The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: systematic subject knowledge, data analysis and writing, project and time management, and collaboration. The actual differences concern objects (courses and students or research and products), assessment (teaching quality and student development or publications, projects and business metrics), and responsibilities (teaching and grading or research conclusions and product validation). First test yourself with deliverable teaching or research materials instead of comparing titles.

Comparisons are based on task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 25-1052.00 page, the adjacent occupation list registered in this evidence route (natural-sciences-managers, biomedical-engineers, biochemists-and-biophysicists, molecular-and-cellular-biologists, chemists), and editorial position boundary explanations. Check entry, appointment and authorization requirements separately against each position's own page and employer policies; this table establishes no statutory duties or qualification rules.

The table compares adjacent positions and occupations: chemists, biochemists and biophysicists, molecular and cellular biologists, natural sciences managers, biomedical engineers and postsecondary physics teachers. Its four columns address the same kinds of questions: what each direction does, its key difference from this occupation, and who is better suited to choose it.

Chemists are primarily assessed on research outputs and generally do not bear systematic course teaching and student development responsibilities; this occupation centers on course teaching and advising, with research as a parallel task.
People seeking long-term laboratory research and outputs suit chemist work; people seeking to turn knowledge into courses and take responsibility for student development suit this occupation.
Conduct chemical research in research institutions or company laboratories, with research reports, publications and patents as the main outputs.
Chemists

Biochemists and biophysicists focus on molecular mechanisms in living systems and more specialized research questions; this occupation's courses cover broader chemical topics such as chemical foundations, analytical chemistry and chemical separation.
People seeking deep work on molecular mechanisms in life sciences suit biochemistry and biophysics; people wishing to teach foundational chemistry courses suit this occupation.
Study chemical and physical mechanisms of biomolecules and life processes, mainly producing research findings and methods.
Biochemists and Biophysicists
Molecular and cellular biologists' training and research objects lean toward biology; this occupation is grounded in chemistry and provides chemistry instruction.
People preferring biological questions and experimental techniques suit molecular and cellular biology; people preferring chemistry, substance properties and analytical methods suit this occupation.
Study biological questions at cellular and molecular levels in laboratories, mainly producing research findings and experimental methods.
Molecular and Cellular Biologists

Natural sciences managers organize work, allocate resources and manage performance, generally no longer teaching daily; this occupation's frontline duties are teaching and advising, with management usually temporary or concurrent.
People seeking team and resource management suit natural sciences management; people wishing to remain in frontline teaching and advising suit this occupation.
Manage research or production teams, budgets and projects, mainly producing team outcomes and business metrics.
Natural Sciences Managers
Biomedical engineers produce engineering devices and validation data and are assessed on products and projects; this occupation produces courses, student development and academic outputs.
People seeking device and product development suit biomedical engineering; people seeking teaching and academic research suit this occupation.
Apply engineering methods to develop and validate biomedical devices and materials, mainly producing devices and solutions.
Biomedical Engineers

Postsecondary physics teachers work with physical laws and experiments, with curricula and laboratory safety management differing from chemistry; this occupation teaches chemistry, substance properties and analytical chemistry.
People preferring physics and experiments suit postsecondary physics teaching; people preferring chemistry, analytical testing and safety management suit this occupation.
Teach physics courses and conduct physics research in higher education, mainly producing courses and research findings.
Physics Teachers, Postsecondary

If you prefer long-term research and outputs, compare chemists and biochemists and biophysicists; for team and resource management, compare natural sciences managers; for engineering and product development, compare biomedical engineers; for physics courses and experiments, compare postsecondary physics teachers. Their entry, appointment and assessment structures differ from this occupation; do not confuse this page's teaching and advising judgments with final authority over research or products.

entries: Suitability signal: you can repeatedly teach the same course to students with different foundations and adapt to feedback, rather than explaining it once solely from your own perspective.
Suitability signal: you are willing to clarify grading criteria and apply them consistently to similar answers despite substantial workloads.

paragraphs: O*NET details list 20 work styles; relatively high scores include intellectual curiosity 91, attention to detail 86, dependability 85, cautiousness 77, integrity 72, achievement 71, and social orientation 69. Consider these with teaching, laboratory and grading tasks, rather than saying there are only seven styles or personality thresholds.

Big Five dimensions are only an editorial reference for describing working styles, without direct mapping of O*NET to individual scale scores. Work context: 50% consider accuracy extremely important, 46% speak publicly daily, 34% report extremely intense competition, and 27% face time pressure daily; these cannot prove personality causes success.

entries: Suitability signal: you habitually write goals and assessment methods for a lesson or experiment and adjust after class.
Suitability signal: you can accept spending substantial time on preparation, office hours and grading, rather than only in laboratories.

paragraphs: A point to watch: interpreting "cautiousness" as "giving students no room for trial and error" hinders laboratory teaching; hands-on work under controlled safety conditions is also part of teaching goals.

No official evidence supports suitability between typological tools such as MBTI and this occupation. This page does not use "which type is best suited to postsecondary chemistry teachers": typologies describe preferences, rather than predicting performance or corresponding to appointments.

entries: Suitability signal: if you enjoy making problems clear, teaching and office hours can give you a sense of achievement.
Suitability signal: if you focus more on research, research and supervising student projects also require ongoing communication and collaboration.

paragraphs: A point to watch: MBTI types are not appointment conditions; this page gives no advice for filtering positions by type.

The Enneagram is likewise not an occupational assessment tool and has no official occupational evidence. An alternative is to test interest through specific behaviors: can you design and deliver a complete goal-oriented lesson under supervision and maintain safety rules in laboratory classes?

entries: Suitability signal: willingness to test yourself by "teach a lesson first and examine feedback" instead of "think everything through first".
Suitability signal: after material errors or inconsistent grading are pointed out, you actively correct them and build habits.

paragraphs: A point to watch: Enneagram interpretations can drift into personality diagnoses; this page does not use them to judge suitability.

O*NET10 basic skills: reading/speaking/writing 78, active learning/listening/critical thinking/learning strategies/monitoring/science 75, mathematics 56; among 25 transferable skills, complex problem solving and instructing 72. Knowledge details have 33 items, with relatively high scores for chemistry 94, English/mathematics 89, and education and training 88, among others, rather than only the nine summary items; these are not personal IQ thresholds.

entries: Suitability signal: you can judge whether an explanation or derivation "skips too many steps" and explain the missing steps.
Suitability signal: you are willing to use learning management systems or spreadsheets for grades and attendance, leaving attention for student advising.

paragraphs: Editorial self-check advice: if chemical calculations, units or dimensions are difficult, build foundations and assess capability through verifiable calculations, explanations and feedback; skill requirement scores do not predict persistent teaching errors or causal effects on teaching quality.

U.S. work context: 82% have face-to-face discussions daily, 98% use email daily, 46% speak publicly daily, and 52% continually have contact with others; activities include teaching 92 and coaching and developing 75. Emotional/conflict feedback behaviors are editorial observation suggestions, rather than measured emotional intelligence scores or causality.

entries: Suitability signal: you can handle student challenges and emotions in class and return discussion to learning goals.
Suitability signal: you are willing to discuss teaching problems with colleagues instead of carrying all course pressures alone.

paragraphs: A point to watch: treating all student problems as attitude problems hides course design or prerequisite foundation issues.
Chemists
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to research analysis, methods or product development and maintain reviewable experimental records.
Editorial caution signal: research, quality/product tasks and industry conditions require further learning; research preferences do not automatically demonstrate suitability.
Natural Sciences Managers
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to coordinate personnel, budgets and research or production projects and build management evidence.
Editorial caution signal: project experience does not automatically confer recruitment, budget or performance authority; build actual management responsibility.
Physics Teachers, Postsecondary
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to research and teach physics courses and experiments, transferring teaching and grading methods.
Editorial caution signal: build physics subject knowledge, research directions and course laboratory systems; chemistry backgrounds do not directly qualify a switch.
Biochemists and Biophysicists
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to research chemical and physical mechanisms of living systems and train in experiments and interpretation.
Editorial caution signal: build living systems techniques and outputs; this occupation may also teach and supervise research, rather than being purely research without teaching.
Molecular and Cellular Biologists
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to research cellular/molecular mechanisms and maintain experimental data, sharing experimental writing habits.
Editorial caution signal: build molecular and cellular experiments and research directions; teaching capabilities cannot replace specialized training.
Biomedical Engineers
Editorial suitability signal: willingness to apply experimental analysis to biomedical device or process design and validation.
Editorial caution signal: build engineering design, validation and product conditions; research/teaching experience does not directly grant engineering authority.
People willing to explain knowledge clearly and repeatedly adapt, remain patient with public speaking and ongoing grading, and take laboratory safety and fair grading seriously.

People unwilling to face public speaking and long-term grading, inclined to avoid safety violations or academic integrity issues, or willing only to research without systematic teaching responsibility.

Switching to chemist work requires building methods/products, quality systems or industry contexts according to targets; this is not a lack of course experience when leaving this occupation.
Shared capabilities: systematic subject knowledge, data analysis and writing, experimental operations and safety awareness.

Editorial judgment: chemical analysis experiments are shared with chemists; switching distance depends on target industries and existing projects. Teaching may remain a duty and is not uniformly excluded.
Lack of specialized training and research experience in molecular mechanisms of living systems.
Shared capabilities: experimental techniques, data recording and analysis, academic writing and collaboration.

Editorial judgment: build living systems research training and direction alignment; existing related research may reduce distance. This occupation may also teach and advise, without promises of research-only work.
Lack of cellular and molecular biology research training and technical experience.
Shared capabilities: experimental design and data processing, literature reading and academic standards.
Editorial judgment: build molecular/cellular experiments and mechanism research; distance depends on existing projects, rather than a fixed large distance inferred from titles.
Lack of experience in team, budget, project and performance management.
Shared capabilities: research organization, standards awareness, communication across departments and report writing.
Editorial judgment: build personnel, budget, performance and project management authorization; managers may also research, and teaching loads depend on actual positions.
Lack of systematic training in engineering device and materials development and validation.
Shared capabilities: data analysis, experimental design, project collaboration and standards awareness.

Editorial judgment: build engineering design, equipment/process validation and product constraints; check education and authority separately, rather than requiring engineering education for every direction.
Lack of training in physics experiments and curricula.
Shared capabilities: teaching and grading, course development, laboratory instruction and safety management.

Editorial judgment: courses, grading and laboratory teaching are transferable, but physics subject knowledge and research directions require further training; chemistry credentials do not automatically secure appointments.
Lack of management experience in institutional teaching systems, education programs and student affairs.
Shared capabilities: teaching quality management, education programs and evaluation systems, and coordination across departments.

Editorial judgment: teaching experience transfers to academic administration, but institutional operations, personnel, budget and student affairs capabilities remain necessary; distance cannot be fixed as small or teaching excluded.
Lack of materials science research training and experience in materials characterization directions.
Shared capabilities: chemical foundations, characterization and analysis methods, academic writing and standards.

Editorial judgment: chemistry, characterization and research records may be shared; build material structure/properties, processing and application capabilities according to existing projects, without guaranteeing no teaching after switching.
